Averages are a planning guide, not a forecast. Rain can affect plans in either season. Check the BMS forecast in the days before you fly.

Dry season and wet season

Visit Barbados, the official tourism site, describes two main seasons: a dry season during the northern hemisphere winter and spring, when temperatures are a little cooler and there is less rain, and a wet season during the northern hemisphere summer and autumn, when days tend to be warmer and rainfall is higher. The BMS normals bear this out. February, March and April each average under 60mm of rain and 9 or fewer rain days, while every month from July to November averages more than 120mm.

The north-east trade winds blow almost every day, which takes the edge off the heat. They also explain why the two sides of the island feel so different. The west coast around Holetown and Speightstown sits in the lee of the island and usually has calmer water, while the Atlantic side at Bathsheba takes the full force of the wind and swell.

Hurricane season

The US National Hurricane Center sets the official Atlantic hurricane season as 1 June to 30 November, and notes that storms sometimes form before or after those dates. It puts the statistical peak of the Atlantic season at 10 September, with most activity between mid-August and mid-October. The UK Foreign Office travel advice for Barbados says the hurricane season normally runs from June to November and tells travellers to monitor local news and the National Hurricane Center.

In practice, if you book between June and November, buy travel insurance that covers weather disruption, keep an eye on the forecast from the BMS and the National Hurricane Center in the week before you travel, and follow official instructions on the island if a storm warning is issued. The emergency contacts page lists the numbers to keep with you.

Sea temperature

Visit Barbados gives ocean temperatures of 26C to 29C (79F to 84F) all year round, so the sea is warm enough for swimming in every month. It is never cold, but the coasts differ in what the water does. The calm bays of the west and the Carlisle Bay area suit snorkelling and swimming with turtles most of the year. The UK Foreign Office warns that currents can be deceptively strong even on some popular south and west coast beaches, that some beaches have no lifeguards or warning flags, and that swimming is not recommended on many east coast beaches. Treat Bathsheba Beach and Cattlewash Beach as places to look at the sea, not to swim in it.

Crowds and prices through the year

Demand follows the northern winter. For a winter trip, compare flights and accommodation early, including west coast hotels around Paynes Bay and Mullins Beach. Check availability for Christmas, New Year and Easter before settling your dates.

May and June are worth comparing with winter dates if your budget is flexible. Check accommodation and festival dates together, especially if you want to stay near the nightlife of St Lawrence Gap and Hastings and Worthing. October and November have the highest average rainfall in the BMS table.

Month-by-month highlights

December to February

The dry season settles in, with highs around 29C and the highest daily sunshine averages in February and March. Independence Day on 30 November opens the season, and Christmas on the island is busy. January brings Barbados Sailing Week, which Visit Barbados lists for 15 to 21 January 2027. February is Holetown Festival month, marking the arrival of the first settlers at Holetown on 17 February 1627; the festival's own site gives 14 to 21 February 2027. If a home Test or one-day series is on, cricket at Kensington Oval is worth a day; check the fixture list before you book. For more detail see our guide to Barbados in winter.

March and April

March is the driest month on the BMS record, and April averages just 8 rain days. The Sandy Lane Gold Cup, run at the Garrison Savannah, is the highlight of horse racing at the Garrison; the 2026 race was on 7 March, and a confirmed 2027 date was not found in the official sources checked as of November 2026. The Oistins Fish Festival takes place every Easter weekend in Oistins; Easter falls on 28 March in 2027. Check school-holiday dates and accommodation availability if travelling at Easter.

May and June

Rain starts to climb, from 74mm in May to just over 100mm in June, and June has the fewest sunshine hours on the record at 7.5 a day. This is good value time for scuba diving, catamaran cruises and sightseeing inland at Harrison's Cave and St Nicholas Abbey. The hurricane season officially starts on 1 June.

July and August

Crop Over, which the National Cultural Foundation describes as a festival of about three months, builds to Kadooment Day, the first Monday in August, with the Grand Kadooment parade. In 2027 that is Monday 2 August. Emancipation Day is commemorated on 1 August; in 2027 its public holiday is observed on Tuesday 3 August under the Public Holidays Act. Expect higher demand and prices around those dates, and book well ahead if the festival is the reason for your trip. Read our Crop Over guide before you plan.

September to November

The wettest stretch of the year and the heart of the hurricane season. Check availability and the forecast rather than assuming quiet beaches or guaranteed sunshine. The Barbados Food and Rum Festival ran from 5 to 8 November in 2026, and Independence Day on 30 November closes the year's calendar of national days.

Which month suits you

For the best odds of dry, sunny beach days, choose February, March or April. For lower prices with mostly fair weather, look at May and early June. For culture and nightlife, aim for late July to early August and Crop Over. For surfing, ask a local surf school about the Atlantic swell at the Soup Bowl on the east coast and where to start if you are new to it. If you plan to travel in the hurricane season, keep your dates flexible and your insurance comprehensive.

Whenever you go, our first-timers guide, the 2027 public holidays list and the weather page will help you plan. To compare where to base yourself, see where to stay in Barbados, and for ideas once you arrive, things to do in Barbados.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best month to visit Barbados?

For weather alone, March is the driest month on the Barbados Meteorological Services 1991 to 2020 record, with 38.9mm of rain over about 8 rain days, and February and April are close behind. These are also peak months, so book early. May is a good compromise between weather and price.

When is hurricane season in Barbados?

The official Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November, according to the US National Hurricane Center, which puts the peak of the season around 10 September. The UK Foreign Office advice for Barbados says the season normally runs from June to November.

What is the rainiest month in Barbados?

October, with an average of 179.6mm of rain on the BMS 1991 to 2020 normals, followed by November at 172.6mm and September at 162.6mm. Monthly averages do not predict conditions on an individual day.

How warm is the sea in Barbados?

Visit Barbados, the official tourism site, gives sea temperatures of 26C to 29C (79F to 84F) all year round. The water is warm enough for swimming in every month, but strong currents on many east coast beaches make them unsafe for swimming.

When is Crop Over?

Crop Over runs for about three months and builds to Kadooment Day, the first Monday in August, with the Grand Kadooment parade. In 2027 Kadooment Day is Monday 2 August. The National Cultural Foundation publishes the full schedule each year.

Is Barbados expensive in winter?

December to April is a popular winter-sun period. Compare flights and accommodation early for Christmas, New Year and Easter, and compare rates with May, June and September to November.

How hot does Barbados get?

Average daily highs range from 29.1C (84F) in January to 31.0C (88F) in September on the BMS normals. The BMS sheet, published in October 2023, lists an extreme of 34.2C on 30 September 2023. Nights stay mild, with average lows of 23C to 25C.

guides.title: Crop Over Barbados: Festival Guide and Grand Kadooment
guides.summary: The NCF describes Crop Over as a three-month festival, with major events in July and early August. Here is what each event is, how visitors join a band, and what the 2027 calendar does and does not show yet.
guides.html:
Crop Over is a major Barbadian festival: several weeks of calypso, soca, costume bands, food and street parties that build to Grand Kadooment, the costumed road march on the Kadooment Day holiday in early August. It is run by the National Cultural Foundation (NCF), the state body that has produced the festival since the 1980s, so check flights and rooms early if you want to attend.

This guide explains where the festival comes from, as the NCF tells it, what the main events are, how visitors join a band or simply watch, and what has and has not been published for 2027. For the event pages themselves, see Crop Over and Grand Kadooment.

What Crop Over is, and where it comes from

Crop Over began as a celebration at the end of the sugar cane harvest. The NCF's own history, "The Crop Over Story", traces it back to the plantations: when the last canes were cut, workers marked the end of the crop with music, food and a procession. Those plantation celebrations dwindled in the 1940s, though the NCF stresses that, contrary to local myth, they did not die out entirely. Former plantation workers interviewed in later decades still remembered cutting the last canes. The NCF associates the large donkey-cart parade crowds with the modern revival.

The modern revival took shape in the 1970s, when a Crop Over Committee was set up with a mandate to revive the summer festival. The NCF dates the decorated cart parade to 1974 and notes that hotels initially provided the floats. In 1983 the National Cultural Foundation was established, and it has produced the festival ever since. Calypso, in the NCF's words, has been at the heartbeat of Crop Over throughout.

The festival also overlaps with Emancipation Day on 1 August, which commemorates the end of slavery, so the closing period carries both celebration and remembrance. When 1 August falls on a Sunday or Monday, the Public Holidays Act provides for the holiday on the following Tuesday, which is 3 August in 2027. To understand the sugar history behind it, a visit to St Nicholas Abbey, Sunbury Plantation House or the Morgan Lewis Windmill adds useful context, as does the Barbados Museum at the Garrison.

Crop Over 2027 dates: what is known

As of November 2026, a confirmed Crop Over 2027 programme was not found in the official sources checked. Kadooment Day is fixed by the Public Holidays Act as the first Monday in August, which is Monday 2 August in 2027. The official festival website, lovecropover.org, launched by the NCF in July 2026, carries the events calendar and lets you add events to a Google Calendar so that changes update automatically; that is the place to watch.

What the 2026 festival shows is the shape to expect. Visit Barbados gave the 2026 festival dates as 3 July to 4 August 2026. Historical 2026 listings, checked as of November 2026, gave the following dates and times:

  • Ceremonial Delivery of the Last Canes Gala: Saturday 4 July 2026, from 2 p.m., Queen's Park, Bridgetown.
  • Pic-O-De-Crop calypso finals: Friday 31 July 2026 at 8 p.m., moved from Kensington Oval to CARIFESTA House, Waterford, St Michael.
  • Foreday Morning Jam: from 1 a.m. to 9 a.m. on Saturday 1 August 2026, from Bridgetown to the Mighty Grynner Highway.
  • Grand Kadooment: Monday 3 August 2026, which was also the Kadooment Day public holiday.
  • Cohobblopot: scheduled for Tuesday 4 August 2026, at the National Botanical Gardens.

In 2026, Kadooment Day was the Monday after Emancipation Day. The 2027 Kadooment Day holiday is Monday 2 August. Wait for the NCF programme to confirm individual event dates and routes before making plans around them. If your dates are flexible, allow for the festival's final week running from the end of July into the first days of August.

The main events

Ceremonial Delivery of the Last Canes

The traditional opening. The NCF describes it as rooted in the plantation tradition that marked the end of the sugar harvest. In 2026 Queen's Park became a cultural village for the afternoon, the Sons of God Apostolic Church offered the traditional Blessing of the Last Canes, and a cultural procession featured stiltwalkers, Shaggy Bears, Mother Sally, Donkey Men and the Barbados Landship. It is a family-friendly way to see the festival's folk characters; check the NCF listing for ticket details.

Calypso tents and Pic-O-De-Crop

Through July, calypsonians perform in tents and compete through semi-finals towards the Pic-O-De-Crop finals, the calypso competition the tourism authority calls one of the most anticipated events on the Crop Over calendar. Expect sharp social and political lyrics; the audience reaction is half the show.

Party Monarch and the soca competitions

The Party Monarch final, with its Power Soca and Sweet Soca categories, is a late-night concert of the season's biggest soca songs. It is the best single event for hearing the year's road anthems before you dance to them at Kadooment.

Foreday Morning Jam

The pre-dawn party in paint, mud and powder. In 2026 the NCF rules had bands assemble at their starting points by 11 p.m. on Friday, setting off at 1 a.m. and finishing by 9 a.m. on the Mighty Grynner Highway. The 2026 rules admitted NCF-registered bands with at least 50 members and required band security. Visitors should check the next edition's rules and each band's package before signing up. Wear clothes and shoes you are happy to ruin.

Grand Kadooment

A culminating parade of the festival. Check the NCF's route announcement for your edition, including the assembly point and finishing area. Its older overview refers to a National Stadium route and 2019 bands, so it should not be used to plan a future parade. Masqueraders in feathered and jewelled costumes dance behind music trucks and moving bars, with entertainment stops along the way.

Cohobblopot

The NCF describes Cohobblopot as a large-scale, multi-act cultural stage production. The NCF scheduled the 2026 production for 4 August at the National Botanical Gardens to close the festival.

How visitors join a Kadooment band

The NCF's 2026 Grand Kadooment rules opened participation to adults aged 18 and over. Check the next edition's eligibility rules before booking. To join a band you buy a costume package directly from one of the registered Kadooment bands. Check the band's costume launch and availability directly. A package normally includes the costume, and the official festival site says most bands also provide drinks, meals, security and entertainment on the road.

  • Choose a band by its music, crowd size and costume style. The NCF site links to its band listings and registration forms, and each band sells through its own channels.
  • Collect the costume from the band's distribution point, following its collection dates and identification requirements.
  • Arrive early at your band's meeting point, as the official site advises.
  • Pack light: the festival's own checklist covers photo ID, phone, portable charger, cash or card, sunscreen, sunglasses, comfortable footwear, a small waist pouch and any personal medication.

Costume prices vary widely by band and section, so compare the bands' own price lists when they open. Our money guide covers paying in Barbados and US dollars.

Watching instead of playing

You do not need a costume to enjoy Kadooment. Spectators should use the announced route and designated viewing areas for that edition. Find a spot with shade early, bring water, and keep a little distance from the music trucks. The road closures that come with the parade mean the official site tells everyone to arrange transport in advance; check current bus and taxi arrangements and plan your return before you set out.

The Bridgetown events sit close to Bridgetown, Hastings and Worthing and St Lawrence Gap, so compare south coast accommodation with your chosen events. The west coast around Holetown is another option to compare. Compare areas in where to stay in Barbados.

Booking pressure and practical tips

If you are travelling for festival week, check flights into Grantley Adams International Airport and rooms alongside the event programme. Book flights and accommodation as soon as the 2027 calendar appears, and buy band costumes when your chosen band launches.

  • Heat and sun. Crop Over falls in the wet season, and outdoor events can mean prolonged sun exposure. Drink water steadily and reapply sunscreen.
  • Weather. The festival also sits inside the Atlantic hurricane season. Read the best time to visit Barbados and keep travel insurance in place.
  • Safety. The UK government's travel advice asks visitors to take particular care around large gatherings, including street and beach parties, especially after dark and during the festival season. Keep valuables to a minimum and stay with your group. Read is Barbados safe for the wider picture.
  • Getting around. Taxis are busy and unmetered, so agree the fare first; see getting around Barbados.
  • Entry. Complete the online immigration and customs form before you fly; see our form guide.
  • Food. Festival food stalls are a good place to try fish cakes, cutters and a cup of mauby, and you can also consider the Oistins Fish Fry for a food outing.

Planning other dates around the festival? See the full events calendar and the Barbados public holidays 2027 guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Crop Over 2027?

A confirmed 2027 programme was not found in the official sources checked as of November 2026. The statutory Kadooment Day holiday is Monday 2 August 2027. In 2026 the festival ran from 3 July to 4 August, with Grand Kadooment on Monday 3 August. Watch lovecropover.org, the NCF's official festival site, for the 2027 dates before booking.

What is Grand Kadooment?

Grand Kadooment is a culminating costumed road march of Crop Over, held on the Kadooment Day public holiday in August. Bands of masqueraders parade behind music trucks. Check the NCF's current route announcement for the start, finish and viewing areas.

Can tourists take part in Kadooment?

Visitors who meet the edition's age and participation rules join by buying a costume package from a registered Kadooment band, collecting the costume before the day, and meeting the band at its start point. Most bands supply drinks, meals and security on the road. Check availability directly when your band launches its costumes.

What is Foreday Morning Jam?

It is the pre-dawn party of Crop Over, with paint, mud and powder. In 2026 it ran from 1 a.m. to 9 a.m. on the Saturday before Kadooment, from Bridgetown to the Mighty Grynner Highway. The 2026 rules required NCF registration, so check the next edition's rules and band listings before joining.

Why is it called Crop Over?

The name comes from the end of the sugar cane crop. According to the National Cultural Foundation, the festival began on the plantations as a celebration when the harvest finished, faded in the 1940s, was revived in the 1970s, and has been produced by the NCF since its creation in 1983.

Is Crop Over suitable for families?

Parts of it are. The Ceremonial Delivery of the Last Canes, with its stiltwalkers and folk characters, suits all ages, and the festival also has a children's parade, Junior Kadooment. For Foreday Morning Jam and late-night fetes, check the organiser's age limits and suitability before taking children.

guides.duration: One to two weeks for the final festival stretch
guides.budget: Budget for travel, accommodation, event tickets and any band costume package

guides.title: Getting Around Barbados: Buses, ZRs, Taxis and Car Hire
guides.summary: Barbados buses, minibuses and ZRs cost BDS$3.50 a ride as of November 2026. Taxis are unmetered with official fares from the airport, and the visitor permit is gone.
guides.html:
Barbados is small enough that nothing is far away, but the roads are narrow, winding and busy, and allow extra time for journeys. You get around by bus, taxi or hire car, and consider a mix: buses along the coasts, a taxi from Grantley Adams International Airport and at night, and a car for a day or two to reach the east coast and the interior.

This guide covers the three kinds of public bus and their single flat fare, the Bridgetown terminals and which coast each serves, how unmetered taxis are priced, which ride-hailing apps work, and what you need to hire and drive a car. Every fare below was read on an official page and is stated as of November 2026.

Three kinds of bus, one fare

Public transport in Barbados runs on three fleets that share the same roads and, in practice, the same fare. Visit Barbados, the island's tourism authority, describes them by colour, which is the easiest way to tell them apart at a stop.

  • Transport Board buses are the large government buses, painted blue with yellow stripes along the sides. They run the main rural and urban routes from the terminals in Bridgetown and Speightstown.
  • Private minibuses are smaller, painted yellow with a blue stripe. They are privately owned and run set routes licensed by the Transport Authority.
  • ZR route taxis are white vans with a maroon stripe and the letters ZR on the number plate. They are also privately owned and operate on designated routes.

The fare is BDS$3.50 per ride as of November 2026. The Transport Board's fare policy is strict: put the exact fare of $3.50 in the farebox when you board, because no change is given. The Government of Barbados visitor page states that minibus fares are the same $3.50 as the Transport Board buses, and the tourism authority's public transport page, which covers all three fleets, simply tells riders to have the BDS$3.50 fare at hand. On minibuses and ZRs you pay the conductor or driver in cash. Carry plenty of Barbados dollar coins; at the 2 to 1 peg the fare works out at US$1.75, so carry the fare in Barbados dollars. Read more about cash and the peg in our currency and money guide.

Children under five travel free on Transport Board buses if they sit on an adult's lap. The Transport Board lists school-uniform exemptions and an ID-based exemption for full-time students without uniform, plus an exemption for old-age pensioners with a Barbados ID card. Check eligibility directly rather than assuming every visitor must pay.

The Transport Board is moving towards cashless fares in stages and has its own journey app, transitbb, for Apple and Android phones, which it describes as still being updated regularly. As of November 2026 the fare policy still asks for cash in the farebox, so do not rely on a card.

Bridgetown terminals and which coast they serve

Many routes radiate from Bridgetown, so the first thing to learn is which terminal serves your side of the island. The Transport Authority publishes the route lists for each terminal on its website.

  • Princess Alice Terminal, on the western edge of the city, is the Transport Board hub for the west coast and the north. Its routes include 1 Speightstown, 1A Boscobelle, 1F St Lucy Church and 1P Porters and Westmoreland. Take one of these for Holetown, Speightstown and beaches such as Paynes Bay and Mullins.
  • Fairchild Street Terminal (the Granville Williams Bus Terminal) is the Transport Board hub for the south and east. Its routes include 6 Bathsheba, 12 Sam Lords Castle, 12D Crane and 13 Silver Sands, plus 1SA back to Speightstown. The Transport Board's 8 October 2026 notice says a temporary security closure had ended and normal operations had resumed. Check for newer service notices before travelling.
  • Cheapside Terminal handles private minibus and ZR routes, including minibuses to Speightstown and Welchman Hall in the centre of the island.
  • Constitution River Terminal handles private minibus and ZR routes to the south east and east, among them minibus routes to the Crane, Sam Lords Castle, Silver Sands and 99 Bathsheba.

Speightstown has its own Transport Board terminal for routes into St Lucy and across to the east, and there is a loading area in Oistins. The busiest corridors for visitors are the Highway 1 run up the west coast and the Highway 7 run along the south coast through Hastings and Worthing and St Lawrence Gap; check the route timetable and allow for delays. For the east coast and the interior, check the return service before setting out.

According to the Transport Board, start times vary by route but the most common first departure is 06:00 as of November 2026, and its route finder and timetables on transportboard.com show scheduled times for each route. Check the timetable for evening and Sunday travel, and arrange a taxi if needed.

How to ride a bus without fuss

  • Flag the bus at a stop marked "To City" or "Out of City"; that tells you the direction of travel.
  • The route board on the front names the end of the line, not every stop. Ask the driver or conductor if they pass your beach or hotel; they are used to the question.
  • ZRs and minibuses play loud music and drive briskly. If you have small children or heavy bags, the blue Transport Board buses are the calmer option.
  • Press the bell or call out a stop in good time. The Transport Board says to use the bell in advance where safe stopping is permitted.
  • From the airport, GAIA Inc. says hourly buses run between the airport and Bridgetown and other selected destinations for BDS$3.50 as of November 2026, from the highway outside the terminal. With large suitcases a taxi is more practical.

Taxis: no meters, official fares

Barbados taxis are unmetered. Both the Government of Barbados and Visit Barbados tell visitors to agree the fare before the ride starts, and the tourism authority adds that fares are quoted in Barbados dollars. Fares are set by the government, and the Ministry of Transport has published a table of revised rates from the airport, which GAIA Inc. displays on its website. At the airport, GAIA asks passengers to use an authorised airport taxi, marked with a yellow "Authorised Taxi" sticker on the side panel, and to collect a trip form from the Taxi Dispatcher before leaving. If you need a van because of extra luggage, the airport and the tourism authority both state that the rate is one and a half times the normal fare.

For trips that do not start at the airport, confirm the price with the driver first. Hotel front desks know the going rate for common runs, such as a dinner trip from the west coast to the Oistins Fish Fry. Many drivers also offer island tours by the hour or by the day, a practical way to see Harrison's Cave, St Nicholas Abbey and the Bathsheba coast in one go without driving.

Ride-hailing apps

Two apps book licensed taxis rather than private cars. Uber announced its launch in Barbados in October 2025 with Uber Taxi, which connects riders with the island's licensed taxi drivers. pickUP Barbados, a local taxi-hailing app listed by Visit Barbados, also books licensed taxis on demand or in advance. Check availability in the app and arrange your return transport before visiting a remote beach in St Lucy or St Philip.

Car hire and the end of the visitor permit

A hire car is the easiest way to explore the east coast, the gardens and gullies of the interior, and the northern tip at St Lucy. GAIA Inc. says three authorised rental car companies operate at the airport, and many island firms deliver to hotels.

The rules changed in 2025. The Barbados Revenue Authority introduced a Car Rental Levy on 15 October 2025, replacing the old Visitor Driving Permit. As of November 2026 the levy is BBD $5.00 per day, up to a maximum of $35.00 per rental (seven days), and it is included in the daily rental charge, so you no longer queue for a separate permit. Some older government and tourism pages still describe the BDS$10 visitor permit; the Revenue Authority's notice is the current rule. Bring your valid home driving licence, which the rental company records on the contract, and check the firm's own age and experience conditions when you book.

Driving on the left, roundabouts and road manners

Barbados drives on the left. The tourism authority reminds visitors that seatbelts are compulsory and that speed limits vary, so follow the posted signs.

  • Roundabouts need care. Follow the signs, lane markings and current Ministry of Transport guidance at each junction.
  • Narrow roads. Away from the highways, roads are often a single car wide with deep gutters at the edge and few pavements. Drive slowly and watch for pedestrians, animals and parked cars.
  • Buses and ZRs may stop suddenly. Leave a gap and do not tailgate.
  • Navigation. Road signs are patchy in the countryside, and many junctions are named after landmarks rather than numbers. A phone map with offline data helps; check your route before setting off.
  • Parking availability varies. Park on the edge of town and walk to the UNESCO-listed historic centre.

For the east coast run, the drive from the west coast to Bathsheba crosses the hilly Scotland District with steep, twisting roads. It is beautiful but slow; allow extra time and avoid driving it for the first time after dark. Our 7-day itinerary shows how to fit a hire-car day into a longer trip.

Which option suits your trip

  • Staying on the south coast (Hastings to Oistins): buses and ZRs along Highway 7 cover the beaches and restaurants. Hire a car for one or two days for the east and north.
  • Staying on the west coast (Holetown to Speightstown): buses along Highway 1 reach the beaches and Bridgetown. A car or a taxi tour helps for the interior.
  • Staying in the south east near The Crane: check bus times before deciding whether to hire a car.
  • First visit, short stay: skip the car and book a taxi tour for one day. Our first-timers guide and the transport overview help you plan.

Choosing a base first makes transport decisions simpler; see where to stay in Barbados and our things to do in Barbados guide for what is worth the trip.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the bus fare in Barbados?

BDS$3.50 per ride as of November 2026, on the blue Transport Board buses and on the private yellow minibuses, according to the Transport Board and the Government of Barbados. Transport Board buses need the exact fare in the farebox because no change is given. The tourism authority's public transport page also tells ZR riders to have the BDS$3.50 fare ready.

What is a ZR in Barbados?

A ZR is a privately owned route taxi: a white van with a maroon stripe and ZR on the number plate. ZRs run fixed numbered routes. Confirm the route and fare with the driver or conductor and ask where to board and alight safely.

Are Barbados taxis metered?

No. Taxis have no meters, and official sources tell visitors to agree the fare before setting off. From the airport, the government's fare table sets the price, for example BDS$74 to Bridgetown and BDS$122 to Holetown or Sandy Lane as of November 2026. Ask for the trip form from the airport Taxi Dispatcher.

Does Uber work in Barbados?

Yes, in a limited form. Uber launched in Barbados in October 2025 with Uber Taxi, which matches riders with licensed taxi drivers rather than private cars. The local app pickUP Barbados also books licensed taxis. Check current availability in the app.

Do I still need a visitor driving permit to drive in Barbados?

No. Since 15 October 2025 the Barbados Revenue Authority's Car Rental Levy has replaced the Visitor Driving Permit. As of November 2026 the levy is BBD $5.00 per day up to $35.00 per rental, collected by the rental company in the daily rate. You still need a valid driving licence from home.

Which side of the road do they drive on in Barbados?

The left. Seatbelts are compulsory, and speed limits vary by road, so watch the signs. Follow the lane markings and signs at roundabouts.

How do I get from the airport to my hotel by bus?

GAIA Inc. says hourly buses run from the highway outside the airport to Bridgetown and other selected destinations for BDS$3.50 as of November 2026. The bus works well with light luggage for the south coast. With suitcases, or for the west coast, an authorised airport taxi at the official fare is simpler.

guides.budget: Buses are cheap; taxis and car hire are the main transport costs

guides.title: Is Barbados Safe? What the Official Advisories Say
guides.summary: The UK FCDO carries no advice against travel to Barbados and the US rates it Level 1. Both flag crime precautions, and the UK warns about strong currents, especially on the east coast.
guides.html:
Most questions about safety in Barbados come down to three things: crime, the sea and the weather. This guide reports what the official travel advisories say, in their own terms and with their dates, rather than offering reassurance or alarm of our own. The main sources are the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) travel advice and the US State Department, plus Barbados government bodies where they speak to a point, all as read in November 2026.

What the official advisories say

SourceStatusDate
UK FCDONo advice against travel to any part of BarbadosUpdated 23 January 2026; still current at 16 November 2026
US State DepartmentLevel 1, Exercise Normal PrecautionsIssued 10 April 2026

UK. The FCDO's Barbados page carries no advice against travel. Its standard opening line applies here as everywhere: "No travel can be guaranteed safe." The January 2026 update removed information about flight disruptions. The FCDO advises travel insurance covering your itinerary, planned activities and expenses in an emergency.

US. The State Department advisory issued on 10 April 2026 places Barbados at Level 1, "Exercise Normal Precautions". It says petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations, and most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, such as purse snatching and pickpocketing. US travellers should read the advisory at travel.state.gov before booking.

Crime: the FCDO's wording

The FCDO says there have been incidents of violent crime in Barbados, including armed robbery, sexual assault, gang-related shootings and carjackings, and that there has been an increase in gang-related murders involving guns. It adds that some incidents have taken place in populated and public areas. It does not name specific districts.

The precautions it lists are these, in its words:

  • make sure your accommodation is secure;
  • take care when walking alone off busy main roads and taking money from ATMs;
  • avoid isolated areas, including beaches, particularly after dark;
  • only use licensed taxis;
  • take particular care around large gatherings, including street and beach parties, especially after dark or during the festival season;
  • do not carry large amounts of cash or wear expensive-looking jewellery;
  • leave valuables and travel documents in a safety deposit box or secure hotel safe.

The festival point matters if you are visiting for Crop Over and Grand Kadooment, or for busy nights such as the Oistins Fish Fry and the bars of St Lawrence Gap. Our Crop Over guide covers planning for the festival period. On terrorism, the FCDO says there is no recent history of terrorism in Barbados but attacks cannot be ruled out.

Sea safety by coast

The FCDO's swimming advice is direct: "Always take great care when swimming." It then makes four points that apply all around the island:

  • currents can be deceptively strong, including on some of the popular beaches on the south and west coasts;
  • some beaches do not have lifeguards or warning flags;
  • existing lifeguard stations are not staffed 24 hours a day;
  • motorised water sports equipment, including jet skis, dive boats on snorkelling tours and catamarans, may operate near the shore.

East coast. The FCDO says swimming is not recommended on many of the east-coast beaches, where currents are particularly strong, and tells visitors to follow local warnings. This is the Atlantic side, around Bathsheba and the Scotland District, with beaches such as Bathsheba (the Soup Bowl), Cattlewash and Bath. Enjoy the views and the walks; enter the water only where local warnings and lifeguards allow.

South and south east. The FCDO's warning about deceptively strong currents explicitly includes popular south coast beaches. Apply this advice along the stretch from Accra (Rockley) Beach to Dover Beach and on round to the more exposed south east, including Crane Beach and Bottom Bay near The Crane. Read flags where they exist, and ask locally where they do not.

West coast. The Caribbean side is also named in the FCDO's current warning, and boats and jet skis can operate near the shore. Apply this advice at beaches such as Carlisle Bay, Paynes Bay and Mullins. If you join swimming with turtles or snorkelling trips, stay close to the operator's boat and briefing area.

Health

The FCDO lists Zika virus, dengue and chikungunya among the health risks in Barbados, all spread by mosquitoes, so pack repellent and protect yourself against mosquito bites. It says the healthcare system is less extensive than the UK's, that the Queen Elizabeth Hospital can cope with many types of treatment, and that serious cases may need medical evacuation. Medical treatment in Barbados can be expensive, and some private clinics may not accept travel insurance as payment, so check their prepayment policies.

On drinking water, Visit Barbados says the water supply, provided by the Barbados Water Authority, is safe to drink. The FCDO's ambulance advice is to dial 511.

Hurricanes and the weather

The FCDO says the hurricane season normally runs from June to November and advises monitoring local news and World Meteorological Organization weather reports for Barbados. If you travel in those months, check forecasts in the days before you fly, keep your airline's contact details to hand, and follow instructions from your hotel and the local authorities if a storm approaches. Our best time to visit Barbados guide covers the seasons, and the weather page has the climate overview.

Driving and taxis

Barbados drives on the left; Visit Barbados reminds visitors that speed limits vary and seatbelts are compulsory. Since 15 October 2025 visitors no longer need a Visitor Driving Permit: the Barbados Revenue Authority says visitors must hold a valid driving licence and present it to the rental company, which now charges a Car Rental Levy of BBD 5 per day, capped at BBD 35 per rental (as of November 2026). The FCDO refers drivers to its general driving abroad guidance.

For taxis, the FCDO says they do not have meters, that there are standard fares for most destinations, and that you should agree the fare in Barbados dollars before you set off. Use licensed taxis only. Our getting around Barbados guide covers buses, taxis and driving in more detail.

Laws visitors break by accident

  • Camouflage. The FCDO says it is illegal for anyone, including children, to wear camouflage clothing. Leave camouflage-pattern clothes and accessories at home.
  • Drugs. The FCDO says it is illegal to possess drugs and there are severe penalties for all drug offences.
  • Other people's bags. Pack your luggage yourself and do not carry anything through customs for anyone else.
  • Customs declarations. The FCDO says there are strict rules about goods brought into and out of Barbados; declare anything that may be prohibited or dutiable on the online immigration and customs form.

For LGBT+ travellers, the FCDO says attitudes in the Caribbean are mostly conservative, and that it is uncommon for opposite or same-sex couples to show affection in public, which may attract unwanted and negative attention.

Emergency numbers

ServiceNumber
Police211
Ambulance511
Fire311

These three numbers appear on both the FCDO's Barbados page and Visit Barbados's medical services page, as of November 2026. For a British national in difficulty, the FCDO's 24-hour line in London is 020 7008 5000, for urgent help if something has happened to a friend or relative abroad. Keep our emergency contacts page saved on your phone.

Planning with the advice in mind

The advisories point to ordinary habits: secure accommodation, licensed taxis, valuables in a safe, care after dark and at big parties, and great care in the sea. Choose a base with our where to stay guide, read the first-timer's guide and the currency and money guide for handling cash, and check our local tips. Families can start from the 7-day family itinerary and apply the sea advice above to every beach day.

What we could not confirm

  • Penalty amounts for wearing camouflage.
  • Whether a particular beach has a lifeguard on duty at the time you visit. Check locally and follow flags.
  • Live sea conditions at individual beaches.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Barbados safe to visit in 2026?

The UK FCDO has no advice against travel to Barbados (updated 23 January 2026, still current on 16 November 2026), and the US State Department advisory issued on 10 April 2026 places Barbados at Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions. The FCDO also reports incidents of violent crime and lists precautions, so follow them.

What level is the US travel advisory for Barbados?

The State Department advisory issued on 10 April 2026 places Barbados at Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions. Check travel.state.gov for updates.

Is it safe to swim on the east coast of Barbados?

The FCDO says swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches, where currents are particularly strong, and to follow local warnings. It also warns that currents can be deceptively strong on some popular south and west coast beaches and that some beaches have no lifeguards or flags.

What precautions does the UK advise in Barbados?

Secure accommodation; care when walking alone off busy main roads and at ATMs; avoiding isolated areas, including beaches, after dark; licensed taxis only; care around large gatherings, especially at night or during festivals; no large amounts of cash or expensive-looking jewellery; and valuables in a safe.

Is it illegal to wear camouflage in Barbados?

Yes. The FCDO says it is illegal for anyone, including children, to wear camouflage clothing in Barbados. Do not pack it.

What are the emergency numbers in Barbados?

Police 211, ambulance 511 and fire 311, as listed by the FCDO and Visit Barbados in November 2026.

When is hurricane season in Barbados?

The FCDO says the hurricane season normally runs from June to November. Monitor local news and World Meteorological Organization weather reports if you travel then.

guides.title: Things to Do in Barbados: A Guide by Interest
guides.summary: Things to do in Barbados by interest: calm west coast beaches, turtle swims in Carlisle Bay, Harrison's Cave, the gullies and gardens, UNESCO-listed Bridgetown, rum distilleries, the wild east coast and Oistins on a Friday.
guides.html:
Barbados is a small island with a lot of variety packed into it. The sheltered west coast faces the Caribbean Sea, the south coast catches the trade winds, and the east coast takes the full force of the Atlantic. Inland, the land rises into limestone ridges cut by deep gullies, with caves underneath and old plantation houses on top. This guide sorts the best things to do by interest, so you can build days around what you like rather than a checklist. Each item links to its own page with practical details.

Beaches, coast by coast

The coast you pick decides the kind of beach day you get. For a full comparison, read our guide to the best beaches in Barbados.

West coast: calm water and snorkelling

The St James and St Peter shoreline is the calm side of the island, usually the best for swimming and snorkelling straight off the sand. Paynes Bay and Sandy Lane Beach are long, sheltered curves; Folkestone Beach sits beside the Folkestone Marine Park near Holetown; Mullins Beach and Gibbes Beach are options further north, and Heywoods Beach runs north of Speightstown.

Carlisle Bay: the beach next to the capital

Just south of Bridgetown, Carlisle Bay includes Pebbles Beach. Brighton Beach is a separate beach off the Spring Garden Highway. The Carlisle Bay Marine Park is known for diving and snorkelling over shipwrecks.

South coast: lively and breezy

The Christ Church coast has more bars and restaurants behind the sand and more wind in front of it. Accra Beach (Rockley Beach) and Dover Beach suit an easy day near cafes. Miami Beach (Enterprise Beach) near Oistins has a calmer side and a rougher side. Silver Sands Beach, near the southern tip, is where the wind picks up and the kitesurfers gather.

South east: cliffs and pink-tinged sand

In St Philip the coast turns wilder. Crane Beach sits below a cliff with waves that roll in hard, while Bottom Bay and Foul Bay are broad, quiet coves. Check access before setting out. Check the sea before swimming here: the Atlantic side has strong currents on many days.

Turtles and the sea

Swimming with turtles is a popular boat trip on the island. Visit Barbados names Carlisle Bay, Holetown, Dover Beach and Drill Hall as the top places to spot sea turtles, and it advises snorkellers that touching or feeding them is not advised. Hawksbill, green and leatherback turtles all occur in Barbados waters, and harvesting turtles or possessing turtle products has been illegal since 1998.

Turtle swims are offered as part of catamaran cruises along the west coast, combined with a stop over the wrecks in Carlisle Bay. If you would rather go at your own pace, snorkelling from the beach works well on calm days on the west coast. Divers have reefs and wrecks a short boat ride away (see scuba diving), and anyone who would rather stay dry can see the reef from a submarine tour out of Bridgetown. Deep-sea fishing charters head offshore for bigger fish.

Caves

Harrison's Cave in the centre of the island is a cave system carved in coral limestone, toured on an electric tram that takes you deep underground. It is one of the best options for mixed-age groups and for a wet afternoon. At the northern tip, the Animal Flower Cave in St Lucy is a sea cave at the edge of the cliffs, with pools and openings looking straight out to the ocean; access to the lower cave depends on the sea that day. As of November 2026, the cave opens Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30am to 4pm, waves permitting.

Gardens and gullies

The interior of Barbados is cut by gullies, steep-sided ravines where forest survived when the surrounding land was cleared for sugar. Several are now gardens you can walk through.

  • Welchman Hall Gully: a long, shaded walk through a gully close to Harrison's Cave, easy to combine in one morning.
  • Hunte's Gardens: a garden planted into a sinkhole, with paths and seating among dense greenery.
  • Flower Forest: trails through a former plantation with views over the hills.
  • Andromeda Botanic Gardens: a hillside garden above the sea near Bathsheba.
  • Turner's Hall Woods and Farley Hill National Park for woodland walking and views of the Scotland District.

Nearby, the Barbados Wildlife Reserve is the place to see green monkeys at close range. For longer walks, see hiking in Barbados.

Bridgetown and the Garrison

The capital and the military Garrison to its south were inscribed together on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2011 as Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison. Start in Bridgetown with the neo-Gothic Parliament Buildings and the Nidhe Israel Synagogue and its museum, then head south to the Garrison. There, George Washington House marks where the future US president stayed as a young man, and the Barbados Museum tells the island's story from its first inhabitants onward. The Garrison Savannah is also where you can watch horse racing.

Rum

Barbados and rum are tied together. The Mount Gay Visitor Centre near Bridgetown offers tastings; the brand dates itself to 1703. In St Philip, Foursquare Rum Distillery is a working distillery that welcomes visitors. In the north, St Nicholas Abbey pairs a Jacobean great house built in 1658 with its own rum and a Victorian steam railway on the estate. Our page on rum tasting and distillery tours compares the options. At the bar, try rum punch, or the non-alcoholic bark drink mauby.

The east coast

The Atlantic side feels like a different island: boulders standing in the surf, empty beaches and hills behind. Bathsheba is the centre, with Bathsheba Beach and its surf break, the Soup Bowl, alongside Bath Beach to the south, where reefs make the water calmer, and the long sweep of Cattlewash to the north. The UK government advises that swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches because currents are particularly strong, so treat this coast as one for walking, photographs and lunch.

On the way, stop at Cherry Tree Hill for the view over the Scotland District, the restored Morgan Lewis Windmill, and Gun Hill Signal Station in the centre of the island for views across to the south coast.

Food and the Friday fish fry

The Oistins Fish Fry in Oistins runs through the week, but Visit Barbados calls Fridays there extra special, with locals and tourists gathering to eat, dance and sing karaoke. Crowds are large and food queues can be long, so arrive early or go on a quieter weekday. Order grilled or fried fish with macaroni pie, and look out for the national dish, cou cou and flying fish.

Elsewhere, try Bajan fish cakes, a cutter (a salt-bread sandwich), pudding and souse and sweet coconut bread. If your dates line up, the Barbados Food and Rum Festival and the Oistins Fish Festival are built around eating.

Sport

  • Cricket at Kensington Oval: a cricket ground in Bridgetown; a match day is one of the best ways to see Barbadians at leisure.
  • Surfing: the south coast has gentler breaks for lessons; the Soup Bowl at Bathsheba is for experienced surfers.
  • Kitesurfing and windsurfing around Silver Sands, where strong winds attract windsurfers and kitesurfers.
  • Golf and polo for a slower afternoon of sport, played or watched.
  • Race days at the Garrison Savannah, including the Sandy Lane Gold Cup.
  • Run Barbados for runners, and Barbados Sailing Week for sailors.

With children

Families can consider the west coast, checking local flags and conditions before children swim. Good days out for children include the tram ride through Harrison's Cave, the monkeys and tortoises at the Barbados Wildlife Reserve, a submarine tour and a turtle snorkel from a catamaran. Ask the operator about boarding arrangements, life jackets and suitability for children before booking. The steam railway at St Nicholas Abbey is a hit with younger children. For a full plan, see the 7-day family itinerary.

A rainy day

Tropical showers in Barbados are often short, but a wet afternoon is the time for indoor or covered sights: Harrison's Cave, the Barbados Museum, the Nidhe Israel Synagogue museum, a tasting at Mount Gay or a tour of Sunbury Plantation House. Check the weather page and our guide to the best time to visit Barbados for the wetter months.

Putting it together

A short stay covers one coast, Bridgetown and a day inland; a week lets you add the east coast, a rum tour and a turtle trip without rushing. Our 5-day itinerary and 7-day itinerary lay out the days, and getting around Barbados explains buses, taxis and car hire. For festival dates, see events, starting with Crop Over in summer and the Holetown Festival.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most popular thing to do in Barbados?

A catamaran trip along the west coast with a turtle swim and a snorkel over the Carlisle Bay wrecks is the classic day out. Visit Barbados lists Carlisle Bay, Holetown, Dover Beach and Drill Hall as the top places to spot turtles.

Can you swim on the east coast of Barbados?

Mostly no. The UK government advises that swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches because the currents are particularly strong, and you should follow local warnings. Visit Bathsheba for the scenery and swim on the west or south coast.

When is the best night for the Oistins Fish Fry?

Friday is the big night, with music, dancing and large crowds. Expect queues for food. If you want a calmer evening, go on another weekday.

Is Bridgetown a UNESCO World Heritage Site?

Yes. Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2011. The property covers the old town centre and the Garrison area to the south, including the Garrison Savannah.

What can you do in Barbados when it rains?

Harrison's Cave, the Barbados Museum, the Nidhe Israel Synagogue museum, rum tastings and plantation houses all keep you mostly under cover. Showers are often brief, so a beach afternoon may still be possible later.

Is it okay to touch the turtles?

No. Visit Barbados advises that touching or feeding the turtles is not advised. Sea turtles are protected in Barbados, and harvesting them or possessing turtle products has been illegal since 1998.
guides.bestTime: December to April for the drier season; check availability for turtle trips, caves and rum tours
guides.budget: Mid-range to high: Barbados is not a cheap island, but beaches, buses and the fish fry keep costs down

guides.title: Where to Stay in Barbados: West, South or East Coast
guides.summary: Choosing where to stay in Barbados: compare the west coast around Holetown and Speightstown, the south coast from Hastings to St Lawrence Gap and Oistins, the Crane, Bathsheba and Bridgetown by traveller type, sea conditions and transport.
guides.html:
Barbados is small enough to tour from any base, but the coast you sleep on shapes every day of the trip: what the sea is like in front of you, how far the restaurants are, and how long you spend in traffic. The island has contrasting coastlines. The west faces the calm Caribbean Sea, the south catches the trade winds and has nightlife, and the east takes the open Atlantic. This guide compares each area by who it suits, what the water is like and how you get around, so you can choose the area before you choose the room.

All flights land at Grantley Adams International Airport (BGI) in Christ Church, on the south side of the island. Compare the route to your accommodation before booking a transfer, allowing for traffic around Bridgetown.

The west coast: Holetown, St James and Speightstown

The west coast is the classic Barbados of calm turquoise water, sunsets over the sea and long, sheltered beaches. It runs north from Bridgetown through St James to St Peter, and it is known for upscale hotels and villas.

Holetown and the St James coast

Holetown is the centre of the west coast, with shops, restaurants and a small-town feel. Nearby beaches include Paynes Bay, Sandy Lane Beach and Folkestone Beach, next to the Folkestone Marine Park. Holetown is also one of the spots Visit Barbados names for seeing sea turtles, so swimming with turtles and snorkelling are easy from here. Every year the Holetown Festival fills the town.

Who it suits: couples, families with young children who want calm water, and anyone whose main plan is swimming and snorkelling. Sea: often sheltered, but check local conditions and flags before swimming. Transport: buses run along the coast road to Bridgetown and Speightstown, taxis are easy to find, and a hire car helps for days inland. Expect traffic on the coast road at busy times.

Speightstown and the north west

Speightstown in St Peter is an old port town, quieter than Holetown, with a waterfront and a more local pace. Beaches nearby include Mullins Beach, Gibbes Beach and Heywoods Beach. It is a west coast base for exploring the north: St Nicholas Abbey, Cherry Tree Hill and the Animal Flower Cave in St Lucy can be visited on outings from here.

Who it suits: travellers who want calm water without the busier Holetown strip, and repeat visitors. Sea: usually calm. Transport: buses link Speightstown with Bridgetown along the coast; for the north and east you will want a car or taxi.

The south coast: Hastings to St Lawrence Gap and Oistins

The Christ Church coast has nightlife and a range of accommodation budgets. It runs east from the edge of Bridgetown, close to the airport, and the beaches face the trade winds, so the water is livelier than on the west coast and the breeze keeps evenings cooler.

Hastings, Rockley and Worthing

Hastings, Rockley and Worthing are the first stretch east of the capital, with a seafront boardwalk, supermarkets, cafes and apartments as well as hotels. Accra Beach (Rockley Beach) is the main beach. This is the most practical area for a first visit or a longer stay: you can walk to food shops, the bus runs often along the main road, and Bridgetown and the Garrison are close.

Who it suits: first-timers, mid-range budgets, longer stays and anyone who wants to manage without a car. Sea: generally swimmable, with more waves than the west; beginners can find gentle surfing spots along this coast.

St Lawrence Gap and Dover

St Lawrence Gap, a short road running parallel to the sea, is the island's main strip of restaurants, bars and live music. Dover Beach sits at one end, and Visit Barbados lists it among the top places to spot turtles.

Who it suits: couples and groups who want dinner and a night out on foot. Light sleepers should ask how close a room is to the bars. Sea: generally swimmable. Transport: on the bus routes along the south coast road; taxis wait in the area at night.

Oistins and Miami Beach

Oistins is a working fishing town best known for the Oistins Fish Fry, which draws large crowds on Friday nights. Staying here or just east of it puts you near Miami Beach (Enterprise Beach) and Silver Sands Beach, a windy part of the south coast popular for kitesurfing and windsurfing. The airport is close by.

Who it suits: food lovers, kitesurfers and travellers who want a more local setting. Sea: varies a lot between beaches, from sheltered to rough, so check before swimming. Transport: buses along the south coast road; a car helps for the beaches further east.

The south east: the Crane and St Philip

Around the Crane in St Philip, the coast turns to cliffs and wide coves. Crane Beach lies below the cliff, and Bottom Bay and Foul Bay are nearby. Inland are Sunbury Plantation House and Foursquare Rum Distillery.

Who it suits: honeymooners, couples and anyone who values space and views over nightlife. Sea: this coast faces the Atlantic, so waves and currents can be strong; check the conditions each day and follow local warnings. Transport: the airport is relatively close, but there is little within walking distance, so plan on a hire car or taxis.

The east coast: Bathsheba and the Scotland District

Bathsheba in St Joseph is the most dramatic place to stay on the island: boulders in the surf, the famous Soup Bowl break at Bathsheba Beach, and the green hills of the Scotland District behind. Accommodation includes guesthouses, boutique hotels and rentals. Andromeda Botanic Gardens is near the village. Separate outings include Turner's Hall Woods and Farley Hill National Park; arrange transport and check the walking route before setting out.

Who it suits: experienced surfers, walkers and travellers who want quiet and scenery more than beach swimming. Sea: the UK government advises that swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches because currents are particularly strong. Reefs shelter parts of Bath Beach, but follow local warnings and treat the sea here with care. Transport: a car is strongly advised; restaurants and shops are few.

Bridgetown

Bridgetown is the capital and the hub of the bus network. Few holidaymakers stay in the centre, but the Garrison area to the south puts you near Carlisle Bay, the Barbados Museum and racing at the Garrison Savannah. Inside the city are the Parliament Buildings and the Nidhe Israel Synagogue, and Kensington Oval is on the edge of town.

Who it suits: business travellers, cricket fans, short stays before or after a cruise, and history lovers. Sea: Carlisle Bay is usually calm and good for snorkelling over wrecks. Transport: buses leave for most of the island from the city terminals; taxis are easy to find.

How to choose

  • Calm swimming and snorkelling: the west coast, Holetown or Speightstown.
  • Nightlife and restaurants on foot: St Lawrence Gap.
  • First visit without a car: Hastings, Rockley and Worthing.
  • Local food and the fish fry: Oistins.
  • Quiet and big views: the Crane, or Bathsheba for the wild side.
  • Families: the west coast for calm water; see the 7-day family itinerary.

You could split a week between a west or south coast base and a night or two on the east coast. Before booking, read the first-timers guide, the list of things to do in Barbados and our advice on getting around Barbados.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the west or south coast better in Barbados?

The west coast is better for calm swimming, snorkelling and a quieter evening. The south coast is better for nightlife, restaurants, a range of accommodation prices. Both have good beaches, so choose on the kind of evening you want.

Where should first-timers stay in Barbados?

Hastings, Rockley and Worthing on the south coast are the easiest first base: buses run often, shops and restaurants are within walking distance, and the airport and Bridgetown are close. Holetown is the easiest west coast choice.

Can I stay in Barbados without a car?

Yes, on the south coast or around Holetown, where buses run along the coast road and taxis are easy to find. The Crane and Bathsheba are hard to manage without a car.

Is it safe to swim at Bathsheba?

Mostly no. The UK government advises that swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches because the currents are particularly strong. Use the east coast for the views and surfing if you are experienced, and swim on the west or south coast.

Which part of Barbados is closest to the airport?

The airport is in Christ Church on the south side of the island, with Oistins and St Lawrence Gap among the nearby south coast bases. Check your accommodation and exact route, allowing for traffic.

Where is the nightlife in Barbados?

St Lawrence Gap on the south coast is the main strip of bars, restaurants and live music. On Friday nights the Oistins Fish Fry is a busy evening gathering, with food, music and dancing.

destinations.name: Bathsheba and the Scotland District
destinations.tagline: The wild Atlantic coast of St Joseph: the Soup Bowl, offshore rocks and green hills
destinations.summary: Bathsheba is the Atlantic side of Barbados: a fishing village in St Joseph with the Soup Bowl surf break, giant offshore rocks and gardens in the green Scotland District.
destinations.html:
Bathsheba is a fishing village on the east coast of Barbados in the parish of St Joseph, and the best place to see the island's second character. While the west and south face the calm Caribbean, the east coast takes the full force of the Atlantic. Waves roll in white across the reef, huge pedestal rocks stand just offshore, and the hills of the Scotland District rise steeply behind the shore. Many visitors come for an afternoon and stay for a night just to watch the sea.

The surf break at Bathsheba, known as the Soup Bowl, has drawn international competitors, and the tourism board notes that swells can rise to over 15 feet. Smaller summer waves suit improving surfers, while the big winter swells are for experienced riders only (see surfing in Barbados). Swimming is a different matter: the UK government advises that swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches, where currents are particularly strong. Rock pools also need local advice: do not assume that low tide makes them safe.

What to do

  • Watch the surfers at the Soup Bowl and walk among the offshore rocks at low tide.
  • Visit the Andromeda Botanic Gardens on the hillside above the village.
  • Drive up through the Scotland District to the Flower Forest and Hunte's Gardens.
  • Walk north along the shore to Cattlewash, or hike in Turners Hall Woods.

The hilly Scotland District extends through the north-east of the island. The tourism board describes the Cotton Tower signal station as having commanding views of it, and Cherry Tree Hill gives another sweeping view down to the coast. Look for Bajan cutters and roast breadfruit on local menus.

Bathsheba is on a bus route, but you can also drive or take a tour from the west or south coasts, crossing the middle of the island past Harrison's Cave or Gun Hill. Stay in the calm-water resorts of Holetown or St Lawrence Gap and come here for the day, or book a night in the village for the sunrise over the Atlantic. Further down the coast, The Crane shows the south-east side of the same ocean.

destinations.name: Bridgetown and the Garrison
destinations.tagline: The UNESCO-listed capital: Careenage, Parliament, Garrison Savannah and Carlisle Bay
destinations.summary: Bridgetown is the capital of Barbados and, with its Garrison, a UNESCO World Heritage property since 2011: a harbour town of historic streets, Parliament and Carlisle Bay.
destinations.html:
Bridgetown sits on the sheltered south-west coast of Barbados in the parish of St Michael, where the Careenage, a narrow inlet and natural harbour, meets the Caribbean Sea. It is the capital and the island's centre of commerce, and in 2011 the old town and the Garrison to the south were inscribed together on the UNESCO World Heritage List as Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison. Buses along both the west and south coasts run into the city, so even visitors staying at the beach can reach it easily.

Two walks cover the heritage. In town, start at the Careenage and the Parliament Buildings, home of a legislature that has met since 1639, then head inland to the Nidhe Israel Synagogue and its museum. South of the centre, the Garrison grew up around the parade ground now called the Garrison Savannah, with the George Washington House and the Barbados Museum in former military buildings close by. Race days at the Savannah (horse racing at the Garrison) are a local institution, and the Sandy Lane Gold Cup is run on the same course.

What to do

  • Walk the Careenage and the Parliament Buildings, then the lanes around the synagogue.
  • Spend a morning at the Garrison: the Barbados Museum and George Washington House.
  • Swim or snorkel over shipwrecks in Carlisle Bay Marine Park, reached from Carlisle Bay or Pebbles Beach.
  • Watch a Test or a T20 at Kensington Oval, or tour the Mount Gay Visitor Centre just north of town.

The water off Bridgetown is the calm Caribbean side of the island. Carlisle Bay curves right past the Garrison with gentle swimming, and further north the city beaches of Brighton Beach and Batts Rock are where many Barbadians take an early dip. That is the opposite of the east coast, where the Atlantic brings powerful surf. Bridgetown itself is a working town rather than a resort: busy on weekday mornings, quiet on Sundays, and best explored on foot with a stop for fish cakes or a cutter. Check local swimming advice even when the water looks calm.

The south-coast strip of Hastings, Rockley and Worthing starts just past the Garrison, with St Lawrence Gap and Oistins further on. Heading north, the coast road runs up the calm St James shore to Holetown and Speightstown. For a first trip, our first-timer's guide and getting around guide explain how the buses fan out from the city.

destinations.name: Hastings, Rockley and Worthing
destinations.tagline: South-coast base with a seafront boardwalk, Accra Beach and easy buses to town
destinations.summary: Hastings, Rockley and Worthing form the first stretch of the south coast in Christ Church: a seafront boardwalk, lifeguarded Accra Beach and buses to Bridgetown.
destinations.html:
Just east of the Garrison, the south coast of Barbados begins with a run of small seaside districts in the parish of Christ Church: Hastings, then Rockley, then Worthing. Together they make one of the most practical bases on the island. Hotels, apartments and guesthouses line the coast road, supermarkets and cafes are on the doorstep, and buses and minibuses pass constantly in both directions between Bridgetown and Oistins.

The Richard Haynes Boardwalk is the thread that ties the area together: a seafront walkway at Hastings that locals use for morning walks, jogging and sunset strolls, with food stalls and benches along the way. It leads towards Accra Beach, also called Rockley Beach, a broad sandy beach with vendors, lifeguards and a mix of visitors and Barbadians. Inland from Worthing, the wetland of the Graeme Hall Nature Sanctuary is a wetland worth knowing about; check our park page for what is currently open to the public before you go.

What to do

  • Walk the boardwalk at Hastings in the early morning or at sunset.
  • Spend a beach day at Accra Beach and watch the bodyboarders when the swell picks up.
  • Take the bus into Bridgetown for the UNESCO old town and the Barbados Museum.
  • Book snorkelling, turtle trips or a catamaran cruise, and ask operators about hotel collection.

The south coast sits on the Caribbean side of the island, so the sea here is usually far gentler than on the Atlantic east coast. It is not always flat, though: the south catches more wind and swell than the sheltered west, which is why Accra has a small surf scene. The UK government advises that currents can be deceptively strong even on popular south and west coast beaches, so swim where the lifeguards are and follow their flags.

Restaurants and nightlife thicken as you continue east to St Lawrence Gap, and the Friday fish fry at Oistins is a short bus ride further. The airport is also along this coast, which keeps arrivals and departures simple. See where to stay in Barbados for how this area compares with the west coast.

destinations.name: Holetown and the St James coast
destinations.tagline: Where English settlers landed in 1627, on the calm west coast of St James
destinations.summary: Holetown is the heart of the St James coast: the site of the first English settlement in 1627, calm Caribbean beaches, Folkestone Marine Park and the Holetown Festival.
destinations.html:
Holetown is the main town on the west coast of Barbados, in the parish of St James, and the place where Barbados's colonial history began. In February 1627 a group of English settlers landed here aboard the William and John, with ten enslaved Africans captured on the voyage, and founded a settlement first named Jamestown after King James I. Today the town is a compact strip of shops, restaurants and the Limegrove Lifestyle Centre, set along the coast that the Barbados tourism board calls the platinum coast.

The coast either side of Holetown is the calm Caribbean shore that most people picture when they think of Barbados: sheltered bays, clear water and sand backed by hotels and villas. Folkestone Beach sits beside the Folkestone Marine Park, where the marine reserve offers reef snorkelling, while the offshore Stavronikita wreck is a separate dive excursion. South of town, Paynes Bay and Sandy Lane Beach are calm swimming bays, and boat trips along this shore stop for swimming with turtles.

What to do

  • Snorkel or dive at the Folkestone Marine Park from Folkestone Beach.
  • Join a catamaran cruise to swim with turtles off Paynes Bay.
  • Come in February for the week-long Holetown Festival of parades, music and food stalls.
  • Drive inland to Harrison's Cave and Welchman Hall Gully, or play golf on the west-coast courses.

The west coast is generally a higher-priced area to stay, with many high-end hotels and villas, but it is also easy to visit cheaply: the beaches have public access paths and the coast road buses run between Bridgetown and Speightstown all day. Sea conditions vary with the weather, and a rum punch at sunset over the Caribbean is part of the ritual. Even on this sheltered side, follow local advice on currents before swimming far out.

Speightstown is a short drive north, and Bridgetown is south along the coast. For the contrast with the wild east coast, take a day trip across the island to Bathsheba. Our where to stay guide compares the west and south coasts.

destinations.name: Oistins
destinations.tagline: Fishing town of the Friday night fish fry and the Easter Oistins Fish Festival
destinations.summary: Oistins is a working fishing town in Christ Church, famous for its Friday night fish fry: grilled and fried fish, music and dominoes beside the boats on the south coast.
destinations.html:
Oistins is a small fishing town on the south coast of Barbados in the parish of Christ Church, built around a fish market, a jetty and a bay where the boats come in. It is a place where people live and work, not a resort, and that is the appeal. On Friday nights the area beside the market fills with stalls cooking fish, music from live bands and DJs, and tables of locals and visitors eating together.

The Oistins Fish Fry is the reason most visitors come. Stalls grill and fry the day's catch to order, usually with sides such as macaroni pie, and dominoes games run at tables alongside. Arrive early in the evening for shorter queues, or later for the music. Every Easter weekend the town also hosts the Oistins Fish Festival, a large community festival with food, music and family activities around the fishing community.

What to do

  • Eat at the Friday night fish fry and stay for the music.
  • Walk out on the jetty, watch the fishing boats and look for turtles in the bay.
  • Browse the handmade crafts sold near the beach.
  • Swim nearby at Miami Beach (Enterprise Beach), or ride east to Silver Sands for the wind-sports scene.

Like the rest of the south coast, Oistins faces the calmer Caribbean side of Barbados. Miami Beach just east of town is popular with families for its calmer side, while the southern tip around Silver Sands catches the trade winds that draw kitesurfers and windsurfers. The open Atlantic of the east coast is a world away, round the corner of the island. On fish fry nights, plan your ride home in advance: taxis and buses are busy when the crowds leave.

Oistins is a short ride from St Lawrence Gap and Hastings and Worthing, and it is close to the airport. Bridgetown is further west along the same coast road. For more Bajan food to try while you are here, see our dishes and drinks.

destinations.name: Speightstown
destinations.tagline: An early major port of Barbados, once called Little Bristol, on the quiet north-west coast
destinations.summary: Speightstown in St Peter was the first major port of Barbados: a small, unhurried town of old buildings, Arlington House Museum and calm west-coast beaches.
destinations.html:
Speightstown is a town in the parish of St Peter, on the north-west coast. It was the island's first major port and commercial centre, and its trade with the English port of Bristol earned it the nickname Little Bristol. It takes its name from William Speight, a member of the island's first Assembly, who once owned the land the town stands on. Today it is a small, unhurried place of narrow streets, old shopfronts and a waterfront where fishing boats pull up on the sand.

The best introduction is Arlington House Museum, a three-storey 18th-century building in the middle of town with interactive displays on the port's history. Around it, the waterfront and esplanade are good for a slow walk and a plate of fish. The beaches south of town are the calm Caribbean side of the island: Mullins Beach and Gibbes Beach for swimming, and Heywoods Beach to the north for long, quiet walks.

What to do

  • Visit Arlington House Museum and walk the old streets and waterfront.
  • Swim at Mullins Beach or Gibbes Beach, or walk the long sands of Heywoods.
  • Drive inland to St Nicholas Abbey, Farley Hill National Park and the Barbados Wildlife Reserve.
  • Book deep-sea fishing or a catamaran trip along the west coast.

Speightstown suits travellers who want the calm sea of the west coast with a local town rather than a resort strip around them. Shops and supermarkets cover the basics, and the coast road buses run south through Holetown to Bridgetown. It is also the natural base for exploring the hilly north: Cherry Tree Hill and the Morgan Lewis Windmill sit on the edge of the Scotland District, where the land drops to the Atlantic.

North of town, the coast turns wilder as it heads into St Lucy and the northern tip, and the east coast at Bathsheba is a scenic drive across the island. Combine Speightstown with a few nights further south to see both the quiet and the busy sides of the west coast.

destinations.name: St Lawrence Gap and Dover
destinations.tagline: The south coast after dark: restaurants, bars and Dover Beach in Christ Church
destinations.summary: St Lawrence Gap is the island's best-known strip for eating out and nightlife, a short road in Christ Church running behind Dover Beach on the calm south coast.
destinations.html:
St Lawrence Gap, usually just called the Gap, is a short road that loops off the main south-coast highway in the parish of Christ Church and runs parallel to the sea. Hotels and apartments sit on the beach side, and restaurants, bars and clubs fill the rest. By day it is quiet and beach-focused. After dark it becomes the south coast's main place to eat out and go out, with street vendors cooking late into the night.

The beach that goes with it is Dover Beach, a wide stretch of pale sand and turquoise water with watersports operators along it. Dover is a good all-round south-coast beach: easy to reach from the Gap's hotels, lively without being packed, and a place to enquire about available watersports. The sea is the calmer Caribbean side of Barbados, though wind and swell can still build on the south coast, and lifeguard flags are the guide to the day's conditions.

What to do

  • Swim and try watersports at Dover Beach.
  • Book dinner in the Gap, then walk the strip for live music and bars.
  • Take a short bus or taxi east to the Friday night fish fry at Oistins.
  • Join a catamaran cruise or dive trip and ask the operator about hotel collection.

The Gap suits couples, groups of friends and anyone who wants restaurants within walking distance of their room. It is less suited to light sleepers on weekend nights, and families often prefer a hotel at the quieter ends of Dover or in Rockley and Worthing. Try local dishes as well as the international menus: macaroni pie, fish cakes and a rum punch turn up on many of them.

Oistins is just east, and Bridgetown a straightforward bus ride west along the coast road. The airport is also on this side of the island. For the full picture of the south coast against the quieter west, read where to stay in Barbados.
